Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:83: From this you can see the greatness of the level of one who occupies himself with Torah from midnight, who deserves to be called "master of Torah," since he unites with the Torah, who is a king's daughter; and certainly, one who persists in this quality will have the secrets of the Torah revealed to him, for a woman reveals her secrets only to her husband.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:84: And the Midrash Va'eleh HaDevarim, on the verse, "For this commandment... it is not too wondrous for you..." (Deuteronomy 30:11), says: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said, to what may this be compared? To a king's daughter whom no one recognized, and the king had one beloved [friend], who would enter the king's presence at every hour, and the king's daughter would stand before him. The king said to him, "See how I cherish you, that no creature recognizes my daughter, yet she stands before you!" So the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: See how beloved you are to Me, that no creature in My palace recognizes the Torah, yet I have given it to you — as it is said, "and it is hidden from the eyes of all living" (Job 28:21); but to you, "it is not too wondrous for you, but the matter is very near to you." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: My children, if the words of Torah are near to you, I too call you "near," as it is written, "for the people of Israel, a people near to Him" (Psalms 148:14) — so far his words. Now, since Torah is likened to a king's daughter, certainly a king's daughter reveals herself more to her beloved at night than by day, for night is the way of modesty, and it is written, "and with the modest is wisdom" (Proverbs 11:2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:85: As appears in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 97b), found in our possession in manuscript, that whoever reads Torah from midnight onward for the sake of unification is called one who occupies himself with Torah "for its own sake." It says there: and there is no one who occupies himself with Torah to raise the Shechinah from exile and to unite her with her husband, for their eyes are sealed and their hearts are closed. And therefore a voice goes forth every night, when the Holy One, blessed be He, descends into the Garden of Eden [where the souls] ascend, and that voice says, "What shall I cry" (Isaiah 40:6)? Go and say that they should occupy themselves with Torah to unite the Shechinah with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the manner of David, who said, "If I give sleep to my eyes... until I find a place for the Lord" (Psalms 132:4-5), and he used to occupy himself with Torah, of which it is said, "and forsake not the Torah of your mother" (Proverbs 1:8) — with her husband, and so on. And it further says: and regarding those who do not occupy themselves with it "for its own sake," the holy spirit, which is the Shechinah, does not rest upon them; and the rest of its wording we quoted in the Gate of Love (ch. 8).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:86: And so it says in the Tikkunim (2a): and regarding those who do not occupy themselves with it "for its own sake," it is said of them, "you shall surely send away the mother [bird]" (Deuteronomy 22:7) — the extra word "et" includes the Name YHVH, which withdraws together with her from that person — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:87: The essential matter of occupying oneself with Torah "for its own sake" is to read it out of love, for we have been commanded several times regarding the commandment of love. When a person rises out of love for the supernal union, and considers how union on earth, with his wife, at midnight, is out of love, so too the love of the Creator should burn in his heart — all the more so if he is a Torah scholar, as we have explained above. And so it says in the Zohar (Parashat Vaera 30a): when the night is divided, those whose longing is to always remember the Holy One, blessed be He, give their hearts no rest, and so on — this being the beloved whose heart burns for his beloved, that he does not slumber or sleep, from the greatness of his love for her.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:88: Although we have elaborated on the greatness of occupying oneself with Torah at night, one must also occupy oneself with it by day, as is explained in the passage we quoted above from Parashat Beshalach (46a), and so it is explained in Midrash Shir HaShirim (Rabbah 5:10), in these words, on the verse, "his locks are curled, black as a raven" (Song of Songs 5:11): Rabbi Azariah said, even things that appear to you to be thorns in the Torah are actually heaps upon heaps — through whom are they preserved? "Black as a raven" — through him who rises early and stays up late [studying]. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish [disagreed]: Rabbi Yochanan said, there is no "song of Torah" except at night — what is the reason? "and rises while it is yet night" (Proverbs 31:15), and it is written, "arise, cry out in the night" (Lamentations 2:19). Rabbi Shimon said, [it is proper] both day and night — because of what is said, "and rises while it is yet night," and "you shall meditate on it day and night" (Joshua 1:8). Reish Lakish said, and so Rabbi Yochanan taught us, that there is no "song of Torah" except at night. Reish Lakish said, when I was tired from Torah study by day, it would give me light at night, as it is written, "and you shall meditate on it day and night" — so far his words. Reish Lakish's statement, "when I was tired... it would give me light," seems to me to have as its mystery the light of a lamp shining within a lantern — like the sun, which withdraws from shining by day and shines by night through the moon and stars: so occupation with Torah by day is the mystery of sunlight, and therefore causes an illumination to be drawn to the neshamah at night. This dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is brought in another form in the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah, end of Parashat Ki Tisa).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:89: Likewise regarding rising at midnight, one who does not occupy himself with Torah with yearning by day, and intend in it the mystery of unification, will not persist in it; and so too in his prayers he should intend the mystery of unification, and when lying down he should contemplate the love of the Shechinah, and consider in his mind when the time of loving union will come to do the will of his Maker — as King David, peace be upon him, said, "I will consider the way that is perfect; when will You come to me..." (Psalms 101:2). And when the neshamah returns to the body at midnight, the Shechinah comes with it, so that she may be unified through that neshamah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:90: Now that we have explained the obligation incumbent upon us to rise, and how great the reward, we wish to explain further arousals based on reason, in order to spur a person on. Rabbeinu Yonah wrote, at the beginning of Sefer HaYirah, that in the morning, when a person awakens from his sleep, it is fitting that he place love for the Creator in his heart, for having done good with him by returning his soul to him, for how many have lain on their beds and not risen! Concerning this we say, "who returns souls to dead bodies" — and then he should not turn back on his bed out of laziness, but should consider how, if he were being summoned to the king's service, how zealously he would rise, or if a fire had broken out in the courtyard. Although his words concern prayer, we should learn from them regarding rising at midnight, for we have already written that at midnight the Holy One, blessed be He, returns the souls to the bodies so that they may occupy themselves with Torah, so that he not have "an excuse for his mouth," and so on; if so, it is fitting to take these mentioned arousals to heart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:91: These two aspects [love and fear] are for the sake of awe, for it is fitting to place upon oneself the fear of Heaven like the fear of flesh and blood — for one who transgresses the king's command deserves punishment. And it is fitting to consider that if he does not repent and rise to occupy himself with Torah, he will fall into the fire of Gehinnom, for every night he does not rise, he is destined to be judged for having blemished his days — since the rectification of the night is through occupation with Torah, and since he has not rectified the attribute of night, his days are found lacking and blemished. You already know what it says in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi 224a), "Woe to him who diminishes his days above," and so on, as we quoted its wording in the Gate of Awe (ch. 10).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:92: And so it is explained regarding the punishment of one who does not rise, there (beginning of Parashat Lech Lecha), in these words: come and see, at the hour midnight is aroused, and the Holy One, blessed be He, enters the Garden of Eden to delight with the righteous, all the trees in the Garden of Eden sing and give praise before Him, as it is written, "then shall the trees of the forest sing before the Lord..." (I Chronicles 16:33), and the herald calls out powerfully and says: to you the supernal holy ones say, which of you enters with your spirit in your ears to hear, and your eyes open to see, and your heart open to know, at that hour, and so on? Woe to those who lie asleep in their holes, not knowing and not considering — will they rise in judgment when an accounting is demanded, and so on — and it elaborates further there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:93: What accounting will a person give if he does not strive to fulfill this matter? Behold it is written, "a son honors his father, and a servant his master; if then I am a father, where is My honor? And if I am a master, where is My fear?" (Malachi 1:6). Behold, we are called "sons" and we are called "servants" — "You are children to the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 14:1); "for the children of Israel are servants to Me, they are My servants" (Leviticus 25:55). Behold, we are obligated to honor our Father in Heaven through the Torah, which is called "the wise shall inherit honor" (Proverbs 3:35), and whoever does not rise to occupy himself with Torah — they said of him that "he does not consider the honor of his Master" — and behold, everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory (Avot 6:12); if so, what benefit is there in his creation, since he does not give honor to his Creator?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:94: And so the aspect of fear — that He is our Master, ruling over us, and in His hand we entrust our souls, and in His hand it is to remove them in an instant, as it is said, "in whose hand is the soul of every living thing" (Job 12:10). And according to the mystical sense, that the attribute of Awe is the Shechinah, and she is the attribute of night, and to her we entrust our souls, one must fear her judgments; and therefore they said in Sanhedrin (92a): Rabbi Elazar said, any house in which words of Torah are not heard at night, fire consumes it, as it is said, "all darkness is hidden for his treasures, a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him who is left (sarid) in his tent" (Job 20:26), and "sarid" refers only to a Torah scholar, as it is said, "and among the survivors (sridim) whom the Lord shall call" (Joel 3:5). This "fire" is not literal, but rather the mystery of the judgment poured out upon him. For this reason, those who occupy themselves with Torah at night are called "those who fear" (yerei'im), and of them it is said, "The Lord favors those who fear Him" (Psalms 147:11), and likewise, "He has given food to those who fear Him" (Psalms 111:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:95: Also among the things one should take to heart is that twice each day we recite the Shema, in which it is written, "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart..." (Deuteronomy 6:5), and part of this love is rising at midnight for the love of the Shechinah, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot 68a) on the verse, "My soul yearns for You in the night" (Isaiah 26:9), and it is written, "I love those who love Me, and those who seek Me diligently shall find Me" (Proverbs 8:17). And so we say, "and be holy unto your God" (Numbers 15:40), and the holiness of a person's driving sleep from his eyes is part of the holinesses — that he should not resemble the people of the world who sleep the whole night, but resemble the people of the supernal world, the holy righteous who rise at midnight to occupy themselves with Torah. And we were warned not to be drawn after the counsel of the evil inclination: "Take heed to yourselves, lest your heart be deceived..." (Deuteronomy 11:16). It follows that whoever does not rise to occupy himself with Torah at night nullifies within himself love, awe, and holiness. And one who indulges in the pleasure of nighttime sleep may be defiled with a seminal emission, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Zohar Parashat Bereshit, end, 19), in these words: further, the pleasures of people who indulge in nighttime sleep — from them come forth demons and female demons — so far his words. And in chapter 18 he explains the reason for this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:96: Further, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, warned us regarding sleep, saying that Torah is acquired with limited sleep (Avot 6:6); and they said in Bereshit Rabbah (44:17), on the verse, "and as the sun was going down..." (Genesis 15:12), in these words: Rabbi Yehoshua of Sichnin, in the name of Rabbi Levi: the beginning of the downfall is sleep — he sleeps and does not study Torah, he sleeps and does not perform his work — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:97: Further, in the Baraita of tractate Kallah (ch. 4), in these words: [one should] be accustomed to receiving all the words of Torah in suffering — we have learned, whoever sustains himself with words of Torah [merely for pleasure], the Torah does not attach itself to him; there it means pleasure of the soul, here it means sleep — so far his words. What is difficult from "whoever sustains himself with words of Torah" is explained to mean one who takes pleasure in himself while occupied with Torah; and so they expounded in Tanchuma, beginning of Parashat Noach, "and it is not found in the land of the living" (Job 28:13) — it is not found by whoever seeks pleasure, but by whoever kills himself over it. And it resolves this by [saying] "there it means pleasure of the soul" — meaning, the verse "it is not found in the land of the living" refers to pleasure of the soul, that is, eating and drinking; while what it says, "be accustomed to receiving the words of Torah," refers to the suffering of driving sleep from one's eyes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:98: And so King Solomon, peace be upon him, warned us of this, saying, "Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you shall be satisfied with bread" (Proverbs 20:13). Although the plain meaning of the verse refers to monetary poverty, it is also explained in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu (Zuta, ch. 14) as referring to poverty of Torah. It says in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, and so on, on this verse: "bread" refers only to Torah, as it is said, "Come, eat of my bread..." (Proverbs 9:5), and it says, "The Lord God has given me the tongue of the learned..." (Isaiah 50:4) — from this you learn that the words of Torah are absorbed only by one who wearies himself with them. So the holy spirit used to inform the Torah scholars, saying: My children, although I have given you good in this world, I need not tell you [how great is the reward] in the World to Come, for you have a great reward — do not treat My Torah with contempt, and do not indulge excessively in eating and drinking — so far his words. The intent of "do not treat My Torah with contempt, and do not indulge excessively..." is because eating brings on sleep, and one who indulges excessively in eating and drinking indulges excessively in sleep, and is thereby found idle from words of Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:99: And so it is understood from the words of Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, just before this, which says, in these words: who impoverishes himself? Whoever indulges excessively in eating and drinking, as it is said, "for the glutton and the drunkard shall come to poverty" (Proverbs 23:21), and it says, "love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes..." and "bread" refers only to Torah, and so on. What connection is there between the verse "love not sleep, lest you come to poverty" and the verse "for the glutton and the drunkard shall come to poverty"? Rather, the intent of "who impoverishes himself" is not about monetary poverty but about poverty of Torah, and it derives this by verbal analogy: just as the verse "love not sleep, lest you come to poverty" refers to poverty of Torah — the proof being from its ending, "open your eyes" — so the verse "for the glutton and the drunkard shall come to poverty" refers to poverty of Torah, for the reason explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:100: It follows that whoever wishes to rise at midnight must not overindulge in heavy eating, which increases sleep, and should likewise be careful not to become drunk on wine, and should not overindulge in drinking water either, for drinking a lot of water naturally increases sleep — especially one who drinks water early in the morning, sleep will increase upon him greatly. Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said regarding Ezekiel, of whom it was said (Ezekiel 4:11), "and you shall drink water by measure, a sixth of a hin from time to time you shall drink" — for a "measure" (mesurah) is a small unit, one-thirtieth of a log; and what it says, "a sixth of a hin," does not mean that the measure is a sixth of a hin, but that he should not drink more than a sixth of a hin from one time to the next, and from that sixth of a hin he should drink by small measure, little by little, so that he not become fully satisfied with water at any one time — so writes the Radak, peace be upon him, in his commentary on the verse. And a sixth of a hin is the equivalent of twelve eggs, since a hin is twelve logs, and a log is six eggs — this is the amount a person should drink from one day to the next, drinking it by measure, little by little; and it is possible that this is what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, intended in saying (Avot 6:4), "and drink water by measure."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:101: Close to this, Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, of blessed memory, wrote in his commentary on the Chapters (Avot, ibid.), in these words: further, bread with salt is good for remembering, whereas water causes forgetting; and one who reclines at the head of the bed, in a bed of damask, finds it difficult to rise in the early morning to study Torah, but one who suffers for the sake of Torah preserves it — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:102: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 21b), on the verse, "I, wisdom, dwell with craftiness (armah)" (Proverbs 8:12): Rabbi Assi bar Chanina said, the words of Torah endure only in one who makes himself naked (arum) for them, as it is said, "I, wisdom, dwell with armah" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:103: Also, one should be content with whatever food he finds ready at night, and not delay until a dish is cooked for him, for then he would nullify the service of his Maker for the sake of his body's pleasure. Also, whoever wishes to fulfill this practice, being among the Torah scholars who abstain from Sabbath night to Sabbath night, must be careful not to eat meat or drink wine at night on the six weekdays, lest he come to arousal and emit seed in vain — unless he fasts, for then he will not come to this, because the affliction of the fast will weaken his strength and he will not come to arousal. This matter depends on each person's nature — there are those whose nature is cold, so that even if they eat meat and drink wine they will not come to arousal, and there are those whose nature is hot; each should examine his own nature and guard himself so that his gain not come at the cost of his loss.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:104: Also, one should take to heart that it is fitting to repent, to rectify the remaining nights of his life, so that he not be called to account for them; and if he repents properly, it is possible that the many nights he blemished by not occupying himself with Torah will not be held against him — but the night in which he did not occupy himself with Torah has passed, and there is no longer any remedy for it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:105: One cannot say that if he did not occupy himself with Torah at night he will do so by day, for where one has blemished, one must rectify there — as it is said in the Zohar (Parashat Pinchas 217a), on the verse, "and hang them up before the Lord against the sun" (Numbers 25:4), in the words of Rabbi Shimon, peace be upon him, in these words: rather, from here we learn: in the place where a person sins against the Holy One, blessed be He, in that same place he must make rectification for his soul. They sinned regarding the holy Covenant, which is called "sun"; therefore the judgment and the rectification are "against the sun" and not in another place. From here [we learn] that a person need not rectify his soul except in that same place where he sinned; and whoever does not do so has no proper rectification ever — so far his words. This shows that where one has blemished, there the rectification must be.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:106: It seems to me that if one has blemished the attribute of night with a seminal emission, his rectification is to drive sleep from his eyes at night through occupation with Torah — that is, when the emission occurs from midnight onward, as explained above regarding "people who indulge in nighttime sleep," and so on. And in order not to have a seminal emission before midnight, it is good that he occupy himself with Torah before lying down, as it says in tractate Berachot (14a): Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, whoever satiates himself with words of Torah and goes to sleep is not brought bad tidings, as it is said, "and he who is satisfied shall rest, he shall not be visited by evil (ra)" (Proverbs 19:23); and it is already known (Zohar Parashat Shelach 158a) that one who emits seed in vain is called "ra" (evil).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:107: Also one should take to heart what the verse says, "My people, what have I done to you, and how have I wearied you? Answer Me" (Micah 6:3). Behold, we see that the king's servants have several types of labor imposed on them, and they work with a good heart and with joy. And it is fitting to consider that if he were a captive — and it is known that captives have a heavy yoke placed upon them — how much more fitting is it that he accept upon himself the yoke of Torah, to rise for the service of our King, even if it be difficult, all the more so since if a master says to his servant, "for love of me, do such and such, to give me satisfaction," how zealously that servant would act! And behold, the Shechinah says, "Companions listen for your voice, let me hear it" (Song of Songs 8:13).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:108: Further, he should consider: if a royal messenger came to summon him to the king's palace, particularly if [the king] is a great prince and honored one, how zealously fitting it would be for him to rise quickly! So too he should consider that his soul, which returns [at midnight] to summon him to rise and occupy himself with Torah, is the king's messenger — especially since the Shechinah herself is the one returning souls at this hour — and it is fitting that he rise with zeal, as a prince and master awaits him. And it is fitting that he rise with joy and love, considering that he stands before the Cause of all causes, before all the righteous who are in the Garden of Eden — for behold, there is no barrier between us and Him, since He returns our souls to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:109: It is fitting for every person to think of the resurrection of the dead effected in him, in the manner of what we say, "who returns souls to dead bodies" — particularly since He returns his soul renewed, as it is said, "new every morning" (Lamentations 3:23); therefore it is fitting that he rise with joy and not consider his rising to be a heavy yoke upon him, for he is punished as it is written, "because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy" (Deuteronomy 28:47). For since he stands before the supernal King and before all His servants and attendants, and the King says to him, "It is My wish that you be among My servants who sing before Me" — who is the wicked servant who would not wish to be among the King's servants? And he should say in his heart, "From where have I merited to be among the members of the King's palace who stand before Him?" And he should consider the abundant goodness of the Creator toward him, as we elaborated in the Gate of Love, chapter 2, and it is fitting that he not be ungrateful, but should be zealous in the service of his King, and consider himself like a servant whose master has already paid him his wage in advance with a gracious face — for it is fitting that the servant be zealous to work in return for the benefit he has received, with a gracious face and out of love. And already known is the statement of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (see Tanchuma, Emor 7), "Who has anticipated Me, that I should repay him?" (Job 41:3), which we quoted in the Gate of Love, chapter 2.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:110: And he should consider that if, upon rising, he were to dig and find a hidden treasure, how zealously he would rise! In this same measure should be the service of the Creator, as it is said, "if you seek it as silver, and search for it as for hidden treasures, then you shall understand the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 2:4). Behold, the good of this world perishes and is lost, while the good of the World to Come stands and endures forever, and the words of Torah are more desirable than gold, than much fine gold.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:111: And if he awakens from his sleep at night and empties his heart of purpose [wasting the time], he becomes liable regarding his own soul, for he is obligated to rise and occupy himself with Torah, and if he does not rise, he mocks the King's reward — similar to what the pious Yavetz, peace be upon him, explains, that "two who sit together without words of Torah between them, this is a session of scorners," which he explains in its place in the Chapters (Avot 3:2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:112: Therefore it is fitting that he rise with zeal and not turn over on his bed out of laziness, thinking about what he has dreamed, so that he go back to sleep — and any dream that is from the side of holiness will not be dominated by forgetfulness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:113: Should you say, but there are indeed those who do not awaken at midnight — one may say this comes from a lack of arousal in their deeds and Torah study. The reason is that when the neshamah returns at night to its place, the Shechinah is aroused through it and adorns herself for unification through the Torah and good deeds one occupied himself with by day, and afterward returns to her place. And so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 213b), in these words: at night one should set his will, for he has departed from this world, and his soul has gone forth from him, and it returns to the Master of all; for on every single night there is a mystery of mysteries for those wise of heart to know — this lower firmament, in the mystery of that point that stands as we have said, that firmament is comprised of above and below, and its foundation (yesod) is below — like this lamp, whose light ascends darkly to unite with the white light, its foundation being below, in that wick with the oil; likewise below, in that point: by day it is comprised from above, at night it is comprised from below, from those souls of the righteous.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:114: And it further says there that the angel Suriah is appointed to bring up the souls of the righteous every night as an offering to the Holy One, blessed be He, and He smells the souls, in the manner that the Messiah King is destined to smell, as it is written, "and he shall smell in the fear of the Lord" (Isaiah 11:3) — the intent being that He smells them and their deeds, [to see] whether they are fit to ascend above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:115: It further says there this mystery to the master of judgment: when this point becomes pregnant, like a woman who becomes pregnant, she enjoys that pleasure that the soul is comprised of, from this world, from those deeds and that Torah he occupied himself with by day, and she takes that will of this world and enjoys it with joy, and is comprised from all sides; afterward she brings them forth outward and gives birth to them anew as before, and the neshamah is now new as before — and this is the mystery of "new every morning" — new, certainly, as stated — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:116: And in the Zohar (Parashat Mishpatim 119b) it says that one's soul must ascend every night through the Torah and mitzvah one occupied himself with by day, and it explains there [the meaning of] Torah, which is the Ten Commandments, and so on, and the mitzvah of tefillin, and so on — see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:117: Likewise one should be careful, before the evening prayer, to precede it with Torah study, as they said (Berachot 4b): a person comes from his work in the evening — if he is accustomed to reading Scripture, he should read; if to studying Mishnah, he should study — and he should not say, "I will eat a little and sleep a little and then pray," for whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:118: The order of the night is as follows: before lying down, one should examine his deeds, what he did that day, and write down his deeds in brief so as not to forget them, to fulfill "and my sin is always before me" (Psalms 51:5), as it is likewise written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 21). And in the Zohar (Parashat Korach 178a), in these words, on the verse, "for there is no deed, nor reckoning, nor knowledge..." (Ecclesiastes 9:10), it says: whoever has good deeds, or is a master of reckoning — we have established that every single night, before he lies down and before he sleeps, a person must make a reckoning of the deeds he did that whole day, and repent of them, and pray for mercy regarding them — why at that hour? Because at that hour the tree of death rests in the world, and all the people of the world taste the taste of death; therefore at that hour he must make a reckoning of his deeds and confess them, because it is the hour of death, and these are called "masters of reckoning" — so far his words. And so it is likewise explained there (Parashat Vayeshev 191a). And regarding the matter of confession, there are further particulars explained in the Zohar (Parashat Tzav, Ra'aya Meheimna, 33a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:119: It is very good that one weep over his sins while confessing his sins, for when his soul ascends through tears, it will certainly ascend above in holiness, since all the gates are locked except for the gates of tears (see Berachot 32b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:120: Afterward he should say, "We beseech You, by the great power of Your right hand, release the bound one," and so on, which contains the Forty-Two-Letter Name in its initial letters, and it is explained in the Tikkunim that the special property of this Name is to raise the soul above and hide it from all the destroying angels. This matter is found in our possession in manuscript (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 94a), in these words: and these seven words, Aleph-Bet-Gimel-Yod-Tav-Tzadi, Kof-Reish-Ayin-Shin-Tet-Nun, Nun-Gimel-Dalet-Yod-Kaf-Shin, Bet-Tet-Reish-Tzadi-Tav-Gimel, Chet-Kof-Bet-Tet-Nun-Ayin, Yod-Gimel-Lamed-Peh-Zayin-Kof, Shin-Kof-Vav-Tzadi-Yod-Tav — concerning them it is said, "six wings, six wings for each one" (Isaiah 6:2), and so on; and this Name is its special property, to cover the soul when it ascends above every single night, to testify concerning a person's good deeds before the destroying angels, and from all harmful spirits, spirits of the night, and demons, and through them it flies above — with two letters of each Name it covers its face from them, and with two letters it covers its feet, and with two letters it flies above; and likewise for the ruach, and likewise for the nefesh (and there is the Forty-Two-Letter Name in the form of a wax seal, and there is the Forty-Two-Letter Name that is the image of the King engraved upon the seal, and there is the Forty-Two-Letter Name that is His own image, [namely] YHVH — Yod-Kei Vav-Kei, Yod-Vav-Dalet Heh-Aleph Vav-Aleph-Vav Heh-Aleph, the Forty-Two-Letter Name being Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh, the depiction of Forty-Two in wax on this text, Alef-Bet-Gimel-Yod-Tav-Tzadi) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:121: After confessing, he should intend to raise up an offering to the Lord, and that his soul make the Shechinah [rise] through "female waters" until midnight, and at midnight the Shechinah will return his soul to him; and this is the intent of "into Your hand I entrust my spirit" (Psalms 31:6).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 7:122: Also, it is fitting to prepare a rooster to wake him at midnight, for we find that Rabbi Akiva, when traveling on the road, would bring a rooster with him, as explained in the chapter HaRo'eh (Berachot 60b). Further, it says in the Zohar (Parashat Lech Lecha 92b), in these words: Rabbi Abba was coming from Tiberias to the house of his father-in-law's village, and Rabbi Yaakov son of Rabbi was with him; they happened upon the village of Tarsha. When he wished to lie down, Rabbi Abba said to the master of the house, "Are there roosters here?" The master of the house said to him, "Why?" He said to him, "Because I stand exactly at midnight..." and so on. This shows that these sages did not rely on their own wisdom and piety to awaken at midnight, but needed assistance — how much more so we.
